tagline.text: A white hilltop lighthouse overlooking the Pacific and Sakahon Beach

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Bote, Bato, Catanduanes (on the hill behind Sakahon Beach)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (guide and transport included, not per person)

children.text: Bote Lighthouse is a white concrete tower about 15 m tall on a hill in Barangay Bote, Bato, on Catanduanes Island. A trail of roughly 30–45 minutes from Sakahon Beach leads to a 360-degree view of the Pacific and the coastline.

Bote Lighthouse stands on a high hill in Barangay Bote, Bato, on the southeastern side of Catanduanes Island in the Bicol region. According to the Lighthouse Directory, it is about 15 m tall, a square white concrete tower with a stairway spiraling around it, and it is recorded as an active aid to navigation showing two white flashes every 10 seconds. No source gives the year it was built, so please confirm its exact history locally.

The appeal lies less in the tower itself than in the walk up and the view from the top. You start at Sakahon Beach at the end of the village road, cross sharp coral rocks and thorny brush, and pull yourself up rope-assisted sections, and after about
30–45 minutes

you reach the tower. From the top you see forest, Sakahon Beach, the bay and the endless Pacific in 360 degrees, and some visitors say that on a clear day you can glimpse the direction of Mayon Volcano.
Bote is a small village of about 1,200 people (2020 census), one of the 27 barangays of Bato. The town center of Bato is only about
8 km

in a straight line from Virac, but Bote lies on the coast behind the hill, so the roads are narrow and quiet. Rather than a polished tourist site, think of it as a place where villagers live and you borrow the scenery for a short while. Greet the people you meet and be courteous when taking photos. One travel blog also notes a PAGASA weather radar station on the nearby hills, built in 2012 with support from JICA. It is a separate facility from the lighthouse, so please follow on-site instructions about entering public installations. The coast nearby also has a landform said to look like a crouching crocodile, so checking the shoreline on a map makes the view more fun.

Catanduanes, known as the Happy Island, is a remote island that sits in the path of typhoons, so check the weather and sea conditions before you plan a visit to Bote Lighthouse. Within Bato there are Bato Church and Maribina Falls, and in neighboring Baras there are Binurong Point and Balacay Point, so they combine well into one day. This guide compares several travel blogs and lighthouse records. Entrance and guide fees change from year to year, so please confirm the latest amounts with the Bato municipal hall, the village outpost in Bote or a local guide before you go.

From the top of the tower you take in the forest of Bote, Sakahon Beach, the headlands and the Pacific horizon all at once. It is windy, so secure your hat and light belongings. Early morning is best for photos, when the sun rises over the sea, while the afternoon light is harsh, so we recommend going in the morning or as the sun gets low.
The square white tower is about
tall with a stairway winding up around it. It is recorded as an active light showing two white flashes every 10 seconds, so remember that it still guards the sea at night.
The trail begins at Sakahon Beach, at the end of the village's cemented road. After enjoying the fine sand and clear water, you cross coral rocks and a forest path up the hill.

blocks.title: Rope sections and coral rock trail

children.text: The start involves climbing over sharp coral rock, followed by several steep stretches where you hold a rope. It is not difficult, but shoes that protect your feet are better than sandals.
Some reviews say the village does not allow visitors to climb alone and requires a guide. Hiring a local guide makes the trail safer and helps the community earn income.
From the beach and the lighthouse area you can see islands such as the Locot group out at sea. The waves are often rough, so it is better to enjoy the islands from a distance.

blocks.title: One stop on a Bato day trip

children.text: You can combine it with Bato Church, Maribina Falls and Binurong Point in Baras, which suits a day with a hired tricycle or motorcycle.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: From Virac to the lighthouse and back

children.text: In Virac town, hire a tricycle or habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) for a half or full day. The center of Bato is about
8 km
from Virac in a straight line.
On arrival in Bote, register at the village outpost or information desk and find a guide. Please confirm the fee and registration charge on the day.
Start from Sakahon Beach and climb to the lighthouse through the coral rock and rope sections. It takes about
30–45 minutes
, so carry plenty of water.
Take photos on top of the tower and enjoy the 360-degree view. It is windy, so be careful on the railings and stairs.
Come down and rest at Sakahon Beach, and dip your feet if the waves allow. Be careful when swimming because the current can be rough.
Return to Virac for lunch.

There is almost no shade at the lighthouse or the beach. Going up early is cooler and gives better photos. If you are back in Virac in the morning, you have the afternoon for sightseeing in town or resting.
Leave Virac and visit Bato Church first.
Trek to the lighthouse from Bote.
After lunch, pick sights within Bato such as Maribina Falls.
Move on to Binurong Point or Balacay Point in Baras to see the coastal cliffs.
Return to Virac before sunset.
The flight from Manila (NAIA) to Virac Airport (VRC) on Catanduanes takes about
1 hour
. Airlines, days and times change often, so check the latest schedule.
From the airport, take a tricycle into town. Bato is reached from the town.
A bus from Pasay or Cubao in Manila to Tabaco in Albay takes about
11–12 hours
, and the 2025–2026 operator-listed fare is about ₱1,200–1,500 for an air-con bus (a non-aircon bus at around ₱835 also exists; fuel surcharges may raise fares, so confirm when booking).
From Tabaco port, passenger boats run to San Andres or Virac in Catanduanes (fares about ₱250–560 depending on the operator). The trip takes around
3–5 hours
, and fast crafts are quicker but run less often. Confirm ferry schedules locally.
Hire a tricycle from Virac toward Bato to reach Sakahon Beach in Bote. Parts of the road may be rough.
A full-day hire is reported at roughly ₱500–1,000, but it varies with destination and bargaining. Sharing the cost by visiting several Bato and Baras sights on the same day is a good idea.
It helps to arrange your ride back in advance, since few vehicles pass through the village.

Catanduanes lies in the path of typhoons and tropical depressions, so in the rainy season both roads and sea turn rough. One local guide recommends March to May and advises against going in the rainy season.
The trek has coral rock and rope sections, so it is slippery right after rain. Some reviews say the trail was damaged after a typhoon, so ask the village about trail conditions before your visit.
Flights are often delayed or canceled by weather, so leave at least a day of slack in your schedule. On summer days midday temperatures often reach around
, so trek in the morning.

and may vary with local conditions.
There are almost no facilities or restaurants in Bote village or at Sakahon Beach. Buy water and snacks in Virac beforehand, and withdraw cash in Virac to be safe. Please confirm facilities locally.

It is easiest to stay and eat in Virac town, where accommodation, restaurants, money changers and ATMs are concentrated, and you can try Catanduanes seafood and coconut dishes. Some travelers base themselves near Puraran Beach, famous for surfing.

For a day trip, have breakfast in Virac and bring a packed lunch or bread and water. The beach village of Puraran has small lodgings and cafes for surfers, which suits a night's stay to continue your trip, but book ahead in peak season.
Go up early. There is almost no shade and the afternoon is very hot.
Wear sneakers or trekking shoes that cover the top of your foot and have firm soles. Some reviewers say aqua shoes were fine.
Carry at least 1 liter of water per person and leave large backpacks in the vehicle to climb light.
Gloves protect your hands on the coral rock and rope sections.
Hire a guide and tip a little to help the village. Confirm the fee before you set out.
It is windy on top, so hold your hat and phone firmly.
Combining Bato Church and Binurong Point in one day reduces travel time.
Take all trash with you and do not pick plants or coral.
Whether you can enter the tower may vary from day to day. If it is locked, do not force your way in; just enjoy the view from below.
Withdraw cash in Virac and prepare small bills. Mobile signal may be weak on some stretches, so download an offline map.
There are coral rock and rope sections, and local rules may change, so check the latest notices and village guidance before you go.
During typhoon season the trail may be damaged or closed. Check the weather and flight and ferry schedules.
Thorny brush and sharp coral rock make shorts and sandals risky.
Reports that the tower door is locked and records that it can be climbed disagree. Follow the situation on site and do not force your way in.
Waves and rip currents at Sakahon Beach can be rough, so be careful when swimming.
Some reviews mention a village rule against climbing alone, so find a guide.
The exact coordinates and trail may differ from the pin on your map app, so ask the villagers.
A coastal cliff viewpoint in neighboring Baras, about
30 minutes
away by vehicle. It is easy to combine on the same day.
A guide to the whole island where Bote Lighthouse is located. Plan Puraran Beach, Maribina Falls and more together.
The starting point of the lighthouse trek, a beach with fine sand and clear water. The waves can be rough.
A church in the same municipality of Bato, good to visit together with the lighthouse.
